name: Infrastructure pivoting
summary: Expand one infrastructure indicator (IP/domain/cert) into its connected footprint, one hop at a time.
description:
A playbook for the Vineyard AI agent that starts from one IP address, domain or certificate and maps the infrastructure connected to it, one verified hop at a time, staging each hop as a node or edge with its evidence. Its central question is whether two indicators share an operator or only a provider.

The pack is text only: it guides how the agent works and runs no code of its own. Every fact still comes from the plugins installed in the project. The pack applies to `infrastructure.ip_address`, `infrastructure.domain`, `infrastructure.certificate` and `infrastructure.autonomous_system` nodes.

## Sections

The agent reads the overview first and loads one section for the hop it is on.

| Section | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| `discipline` | How much a shared attribute is worth and when to stop: the edge threshold, evidence labels versus conclusions, the rarity estimate, independence, and the challenge before asserting a shared operator. |
| `background-values` | Values that recur across unrelated parties: privacy-service registrant names and addresses, managed DNS and mail products, third-party script hosts, generic subdomain labels, default page titles and favicons, and certificates shipped with software (such as Cobalt Strike's default HTTPS certificate). The list is illustrative, not a filter. |
| `prioritize` | Which seed to expand first when there are many: rarity, recency, and how many unexpanded types it touches; one chain finished before the next; how to design searches and keep counts per axis. |
| `settle` | A candidate with a gap: a table of gaps and the check that decides each, from comparing certificate fingerprints to asking RDAP who holds an IP range. |
| `dns-pivot` | A/AAAA, NS, MX, CNAME and TXT from a domain; PTR and passive DNS from an IP. Domains that resolve to the same IP are staged as candidates, with no edge between them. |
| `cert-pivot` | SANs, certificate-transparency searches by fingerprint and by domain, and whether a self-signed certificate was made by the operator or shipped with the software. |
| `asn-pivot` | The announcing AS, its other prefixes as a search space, and a size test before a shared AS is treated as a cluster. |
| `web-footprint` | Build fingerprints (favicon, header-set and DOM hashes) and the account identifiers in a page's markup that show who is paid for its traffic. |
| `cdn-origin` | Finding the origin behind a CDN or WAF through passive routes, then confirming that it serves the site. |
| `historical` | Wayback snapshots for pre-CDN records, defacements, kit changes and old contacts, with every edge dated. |

## How it decides that a shared attribute means something

There is no fixed list of what counts. A shared attribute links two things only to the extent that it is rare.

- The agent asks how many unrelated parties have the attribute, names the basis, and measures where it can: how many domains a nameserver serves, how many prefixes an AS announces, how many hosts present a certificate.
- Attributes multiply only where they could have come from different acts. One hosting panel sets nameservers, mail records and certificate in one click, so "two of three fingerprints match" is usually one fact seen twice.
- An edge needs a tool result that names both endpoints together: a DNS record, a shared certificate fingerprint, an announcing AS, a registry allocation. Edges are labelled for the observation ("resolves to", "shares certificate", "announced by"); "same actor" and "operated by" are conclusions left to the analyst.
- Before asserting a shared operator, the agent passes the evidence to `challenge_claim`, an independent sceptic that names innocent explanations such as a reseller, a shared panel, a copied template or a range that changed hands. A REFUTED verdict withdraws the claim and whatever was added only to support it.

## Requirements

- No plugin pack is required (`requires` is empty); the pack works with whatever collection plugins the project has, such as DNS, RDAP, certificate transparency, ASN, web probe and Wayback. A hop with no installed plugin is named as a hop not taken, never filled from memory.
- Some sections name specific packs: Web Recon (desktop only) for build hashes, Ad Tags (desktop only) for account identifiers in markup, and Wayback Machine for snapshots.
- Graph write access, to stage nodes and edges.

## What contacts the target

Passive hops go through the collection plugins and the services behind them. The `cdn-origin` section also lists active checks that reach the target itself: a direct request with the site's Host header, port sweeps, a /24 sweep around a confirmed candidate, request shaping against the front, AXFR or NSEC walks against the authoritative nameserver, EDNS client-subnet queries and traceroute. These run only in the desktop app, with the analyst's command and probe tools enabled, at the analyst's explicit instruction, and only against a target the analyst is authorised to test. Without all four, the agent names the hop as not taken.

## Starters

Ready-made prompts, each with blanks to fill before sending.

| Category | Starter | Asks for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expand | Expand one indicator | an IP, domain or certificate, and optionally what is already known |
| Expand | Map a domain | a domain |
| Expand | Start from a certificate | a certificate fingerprint or host |
| Expand | Explore an AS neighbourhood | an ASN or an IP inside it |
| Expand | Triage a list of indicators | a list of indicators, one hop each |
| Expand | Fingerprint a URL | a URL |
| Expand | Find the origin behind a CDN | a host |
| Expand | What did it look like before? | a URL or domain, and optionally a date |
| Corroborate | Related, or just shared hosting? | two indicators |
| Corroborate | Check a link the project already draws | the two ends and the edge label |
| Corroborate | Strip out shared-hosting noise | no input; reviews the whole project |
| Report | Summarise the footprint | the starting indicator |
| Report | What is left to check? | no input |

## Report

Every run ends in five parts: what the evidence establishes; what is a candidate, and the check that would settle it; what was deliberately not linked, and why; what was run and returned nothing, named one by one; and what nothing installed in the project can reach. The fourth part lets a reader tell "searched and found nothing" from "did not search".

## Cautions

- A shared provider is not a shared operator. A hyperscaler AS, a CDN front, managed DNS, a mainstream mail product or a common CA groups nobody; co-resolving domains are candidates, not links.
- A shared issuer such as Let's Encrypt is not a link; a matching SHA-256 fingerprint is. A self-signed certificate is either one of the strongest links or no link at all, depending on whether the operator generated it or it shipped with the software. Certificate-transparency logs do not record self-signed certificates, so they cannot count them.
- A phishing kit is sold, leaked and copied, so a shared build never stages "same operator". A stock favicon groups nobody however exactly it matches.
- An analytics or tag-manager token on more than about 15 sites is likely an agency's account installed across its clients and is reported as AGENCY-SUSPECT, not merged on. A money account (advertising, affiliate, payment) can carry more sites before the innocent explanation wins; above about 40 it looks like a reseller or network.
- Identifiers declared in files at fixed paths (/ads.txt, /app-ads.txt, /.well-known/) are the operator's own claim; tags in markup can be injected. Absence from /.well-known/ means nothing.
- A snapshot speaks for its date, not for today, and a defacement is evidence of the past, not of the current operator.
- One turn usually reaches about three hops. A branch stops when the next hop would only reach a value that groups nobody; the run stops when the frontier is empty or the budget is spent, and the report says which.
- When a hop produces a person, an email address, a handle or an account, the agent stops and hands off to the Account & identity pivoting skill pack.

## Source

https://github.com/Vineyard-Intelligence/skillpack-infrastructure-pivoting (file `skillpacks/infra-pivot.skill.json`). Licence: MIT.

overview:
# Infrastructure pivoting

## What this pack does

Turns one infrastructure indicator (an IP, a domain, a certificate) into the infrastructure connected to it, one verified hop at a time. Each hop is staged as a node or edge with its evidence.

## When to use

- The analyst gives you one indicator and asks what else is connected to it.
- You need to expand a lead into hosting, DNS, certificates, ASN, web fingerprints, origin, or history.
- You need to decide whether two indicators share an operator or only a provider.
- You need a repeatable way to record what was checked, what was found, and what could not be reached.

## Do not use

- The analyst wants one specific fact about one node. Run the matching collection plugin instead.
- The question is about a person, an account, a handle, or an email address. Use "Account & identity pivoting".
- No installed plugin covers the hop and the answer would come from memory.

## Requirements

- Collection plugins for the hops you take: DNS, RDAP, certificate transparency, ASN, web probe, Wayback. `requires` is empty because the pack works with whatever the project has.
- Graph write access to stage nodes and edges.
- The analyst's scope and authorization for any active check. Active checks are desktop-only and run only on request.

## Data rules

- Facts come from plugins, not memory. A plugin's `consumes` is its input, not what it creates. A collector consumes one type and produces another.
- Ask list_plugins for the type you want produced, or read the producers in a 0-result answer, before concluding that no plugin covers the hop.
- Use your knowledge for judgements: how common a provider is, which hop to take next, what an unusual record probably means. It decides what to check, not what is true.

## Structure

Load one section for the hop you are on. Each section is self-contained.

| Section | Load when |
| --- | --- |
| `"discipline"` | Before staging an edge, closing a cluster, or asserting a shared operator. |
| `"background-values"` | A shared value looks specific and you need to know whether it is background. |
| `"dns-pivot"` | You have a domain or IP and need its DNS records or co-residents. |
| `"cert-pivot"` | You have a certificate, host, or CT-log result. |
| `"asn-pivot"` | You have an IP and need its ASN, prefixes, or size. |
| `"web-footprint"` | You have a URL and need its build or the accounts behind it. |
| `"cdn-origin"` | A host is behind a CDN/WAF and you need the origin. |
| `"historical"` | Old snapshots matter: pre-CDN, defacement, contacts, or kit evolution. |
| `"prioritize"` | You have many indicators or a limited query budget. |
| `"settle"` | A candidate has a gap and one check would decide it. |

## Workflow

1. Resolve. Turn the indicator into its immediate records or attributes: A/AAAA, PTR, ASN, certificate, or the URL's content.
2. Pivot. Choose the next attribute that is rare enough to narrow the population. Load the section for that hop.
3. Corroborate. Stage an edge only when a tool result names both endpoints. Label it for the evidence, not the conclusion.
4. Branch. Stage candidates separately and name the check that would promote each one. Stop when the next hop would only reach background values.
5. Report. Use the five-part format below, and name the hops you could not take.

## Report format

1. What the evidence establishes.
2. What is a candidate and the check that would settle it.
3. What you deliberately did not link, and why.
4. What you ran that returned nothing, named one by one.
5. What nothing installed here can reach.

The fourth part is the one people leave out. Without it, a reader cannot tell "we searched and found nothing" from "we did not search". A clean report can then look stronger than it is. Name the hop, the plugin, and the seed you ran it on. An empty result is still a finding.

## Stop conditions

- Stop a branch when the next hop would only reach a value that groups nobody.
- Stop the run when the frontier is empty or the budget is spent. Say which, and name the frontier you did not expand.
- Depth is a judgement: one turn usually reaches about three hops. A chain that is still narrowing may be worth another; a chain that has reached a hyperscaler was finished one hop earlier. The analyst decides whether to spend more.
- Stop and hand off when a hop produces a person, an email address, a handle, or an account.
- Never fill a missing plugin result from memory.

## Handoff

When the evidence points to a person, an account, or a handle, stop this pack and load "Account & identity pivoting".

sections.summary: How much a shared attribute is worth, and when to stop.
sections.body:
# Discipline

## Purpose

Decide whether a shared attribute is evidence of a link, how much it is worth, and when to stop.

## When to use

- Before staging any edge.
- When two indicators share a value and you need to know whether it means anything.
- Before closing a cluster or asserting a shared operator.
- When deciding whether another hop is worth taking.

## Procedure

1. Edge threshold. Stage an edge only when a tool result names both endpoints together: a DNS record, a shared certificate fingerprint, an announcing AS, or a registry allocation. One such result is enough. Proximity, plausibility, and two facts that fit the same story are not enough.
2. Evidence label. "resolves to", "shares certificate", and "announced by" are observations. "same actor", "operated by", and "belongs to" are conclusions for the analyst.
3. Rarity. Ask: if these two were unrelated, how likely is it that they would share this? In other words, how many unrelated parties have the attribute? Name the basis so the analyst can check it.
4. Measure. Count domains served, prefixes announced, or hosts presenting the certificate. Use a number, not an adjective.
5. Population closure. "N hosts and no more" claims every axis at once. Count the rare shared attributes the graph already holds, or leave the population open and name the axes you did not count.
6. Independence. Attributes multiply only where they could have come from different acts. One hosting panel that sets nameservers, mail records, and certificate in one click is one decision seen three ways, not three agreements.
7. Challenge. Pass the full evidence to `challenge_claim`. An independent sceptic names the innocent explanations that fit the same facts: a reseller, a shared panel, a copied template, a range that changed hands. A REFUTED verdict withdraws the claim and anything added only to support it.
8. Separate changes. Make each hop a small, separate, labelled change with its own evidence. Do not say a change is "waiting for review"; you are not told whether changes are held or applied.

## Rules

- No tool result naming both endpoints -> stage the node and the check, not the edge.
- Sold to millions -> groups nobody. Mid-sized or regional provider, or shared hosting -> thousands, worth only in combination. Self-hosted or niche nameserver, small operator AS, operator-made certificate, rare reused token -> a handful.
- Evidence words for edges; conclusion words for the analyst.
- One axis is not the population. Count it or leave it open.
- Same act -> one fact; different acts -> multiply.
- REFUTED -> withdraw the claim and its support.
- A junction that groups nobody is noise, not a finding. Leave it unstaged, or remove it and say so.

## Output

- A staged edge with an evidence label, or a node plus the check that would settle it.
- A named population estimate and its basis.
- A stop decision: branch stopped, run stopped, or handed off.

## Pitfalls

- Proximity or plausibility treated as evidence.
- A shared provider treated as an operator link.
- One axis counted and the population called closed.
- Attributes from one act multiplied as if independent.
- A conclusion label ("same actor") staged as if it were evidence.
- A hop that only makes sense inside a batch.

## Example

```text
evil.test and shop.test both resolve to 104.21.0.1, and both certificates were issued by Let's Encrypt.
WRONG: an edge from evil.test to shop.test labelled "same actor". Both facts are true, but the conclusion is invented.
RIGHT: two "resolves to" edges to one IP node, and a note that 104.21.0.1 is a Cloudflare front with millions of customers, so co-residence groups nobody here. Let's Encrypt is the same issue at the certificate layer. There is no edge between the two domains.
What would settle it: the same certificate fingerprint on both, a shared self-hosted nameserver, or one domain's WHOIS naming the other's registrant.
```

## See also

- "background-values" for recurring values that are not operator links.
- "settle" for a candidate with a gap.

sections.summary: Recurring values that group nobody. Check them before staging an operator link.
sections.body:
# Background values

## Purpose

A reference list of values that recur across unrelated parties. Use it to avoid staging an operator link on a value that identifies a provider, a service, or a default.

## When to use

- A shared value looks specific: a registrant name, an email, a nameserver, an MX, a third-party host, a subdomain label, a page title, a favicon, or a certificate.
- You are about to stage an edge based on one of those values.
- You need to explain why a shared value is background.

## Check these values

- Registrant name or organisation: redacted, privacy, private registration, domain admin, domain administrator, whois, proxy, not disclosed, withheld, data protected, statutory masking -> a placeholder, not a party. Linking on one makes every domain at that registrar one fictional operator.
- Registrant email: any address at domainsbyproxy.com, withheldforprivacy.com, contactprivacy.com, privacyprotect.org, whoisguard, or perfectprivacy, or a role mailbox such as abuse@, hostmaster@, postmaster@, registrar@, noc@, or proxy@ -> the registrar's customer list, not one operator's domains.
- Nameservers: awsdns, ns.cloudflare.com, domaincontrol.com, registrar-servers.com, nsone.net, dnspod.net, azure-dns, googledomains.com -> a DNS vendor.
- MX: aspmx.l.google.com and the rest of l.google.com, protection.outlook.com, secureserver.net, zoho.com, sendgrid.net, mailgun.org, pphosted.com, mimecast.com -> a mail product.
- Third-party hosts: sentry.io, hotjar.com, clarity.ms, segment.io, mixpanel.com, amplitude.com, newrelic.com, bugsnag.com, intercom.io, jsdelivr.net, unpkg.com, wixpress.com, shopify.com, squarespace.com, webflow.com -> a service the page calls, not the operator's backend.
- Subdomain labels: api, cdn, mail, www, app, admin, portal, login, static, assets, ns1, mx, dev, staging -> a service name, not a build.
- Page titles and favicons: "Home", "Index", "Welcome to nginx!", "Apache2 Ubuntu Default Page: It works", "Just another WordPress site", "Example Domain", and the stock icon of any hosted site builder -> the software and every tenant who never changed it.
- Shipped certificates: a C2 framework's stock certificate (Cobalt Strike's default HTTPS certificate: serial 146473198, every subject field blank), a certificate and key built into every unit of a device model's firmware, or a product's default localhost certificate -> the software and every operator who never replaced it.

## What to do

- If it matches, treat it as background and do not stage an operator edge.
- If it does not match, run the rarity question in "discipline".
- If the value is a candidate, name the count or check that would promote it.

## Pitfalls

- The list is illustrative, not a filter. A value not on it can still be background.
- A specific hostname can still be shared.
- A default certificate can look strong because the fingerprint matches exactly.
- A shared value can be a consequence of another shared value: "both in KR" adds nothing to "both at that provider".

## Example

```text
Two hosts share an MX at protection.outlook.com.
WRONG: an edge labelled "same operator".
RIGHT: a note that both use a managed mail product; no edge. If the two also share a rare self-hosted nameserver or a certificate fingerprint, test those separately.
```

## See also

- "discipline" for the rarity test and the edge threshold.
- "settle" for a candidate whose value is not on this list.

sections.summary: When you have many indicators: which seed to expand first, and why.
sections.body:
# Prioritize

## Purpose

Choose which indicators to expand first when you hold many, and which searches are worth running.

## When to use

- The project has more indicators than you can expand in one turn.
- A report, campaign email, or collection returns a list.
- You need to spend a limited query budget.

## Procedure

1. Rank by rarity. Use the question in "discipline": how many unrelated parties have this attribute? A consumer-ISP IP or a self-hosted nameserver narrows more than an AWS address. A niche TLD or an unusual domain structure narrows more than a dictionary word on a registrar's sale page.
2. Check recency. An indicator from last week is a live lead. One from a two-year-old report is a check, not a chain.
3. Check touch. Prefer the seed that connects the most unexpanded types: a domain that resolves, serves a fingerprint, and has a certificate expands three ways; an IP that only hosts a parked page expands one.
4. Expand one seed at a time. Finish the chain before starting the next. Do not wait for a review; one may never come.
5. Design one search before many. Each query must be able to change the next action. Do not search a value the graph already holds; do not search one value alone when several values OR into one query; do not search one axis alone when the axes OR into the same union.
6. Keep counts separate. Counts stay one query per axis, because one query carries one result cap and a merged query undercounts. Pay for counts only when a closure needs them.
7. Attribute a hit. Before staging anything, attribute the hit to its axis with a per-axis query or a direct look at the host.

## Search rules

- A value you have not tried is a new question, however similar it looks.
- Same-field values -> OR into one query.
- Different fields -> separate queries; a union answers "something matched", not which axis.
- Counts -> one query per axis, only for rare axes that would change the result.
- Free routes first; the credited engine for what only it can answer.

## Output

- A ranked seed list with the reason for each.
- One finished chain, not a pile of half-pivoted ones.
- A list of queries run, with the axis each one attributed.

## Pitfalls

- Pivoting everything and producing a wall of candidates.
- Leaving chains half-finished.
- Merging fields or axes and undercounting.
- Paying for counts that do not change the decision.

## Example

```text
40 phishing URLs, all behind the same CDN, from one campaign email.
WRONG: pivot all 40. You get forty chains that all resolve to the same background front.
RIGHT: group them by fingerprint first (web-footprint: same DOM skeleton means the same kit). Pivot one URL per cluster and record the rest as "same cluster" candidates. The CDN front is background; the clusters are the signal.
```

## See also

- "discipline" for the rarity test.
- "settle" for a candidate that needs a check.

sections.summary: A candidate with a gap: the check that decides it.
sections.body:
# Settle

## Purpose

Turn a candidate with a gap into a decision, or name the hop that cannot be taken.

## When to use

- A candidate is staged but not linked.
- A label is uncertain or claims more than the evidence.
- A branch is about to close and one check would decide it.

## Check table

| gap | check | source |
|-----|-------|--------|
| same certificate, or same issuer | compare leaf SHA-256 fingerprints | certificate hop, CT logs |
| is this nameserver niche? | how many domains does it serve? | reverse-NS, CT enumeration |
| is this AS actually small? | how many prefixes does it announce? | ASN hop |
| what is behind the front? | old A records, snapshots, cert SANs | historical, cert, CT subdomains |
| same build, or same template? | dom_hash and header set, not favicon | web-fingerprint hops |
| who registered it, and when? | registrant, creation and update dates | RDAP/WHOIS hop |
| is this still true today? | resolve it again now | DNS hop |
| when did this start? | first-seen dates, earliest snapshot | CT logs, archive |
| is this range even theirs? | allocation and its holder | RDAP for the IP |

## Procedure

1. Name the gap. State the one observation that would turn the candidate into a link or kill it.
2. Name the check. Use the table. Prefer the check that settles the most candidates at once.
3. Run the check. Do not report the gap while you hold a tool that could fill it.
4. Record the result. Promote the candidate, kill it, or name the hop you cannot take as the fourth part of the report.

## Output

- A promoted edge, a killed branch, or a named hop that cannot be taken.
- The evidence and the date for any promoted edge.
- An empty check is a result. Record it so nobody, including you next turn, pays for it again.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting a gap while holding the tool.
- Chasing one host through four hops instead of checking forty at once.
- Treating a hedged verdict as a finding.

## See also

- "discipline" for the evidence threshold.
- "background-values" if the gap is a shared value.

sections.summary: From a domain/IP: resolution, reverse DNS, and the records that expand it.
sections.body:
# DNS pivot

## Purpose

Turn a domain or IP into its DNS records and the records that expand it.

## When to use

- You have a domain and need its hosting IPs, nameservers, mail, aliases, or TXT tokens.
- You have an IP and need a PTR, passive-DNS co-residents, or the domains that resolved there.

## Procedure

1. From a domain, collect A/AAAA, NS, MX, CNAME, and TXT.
2. From an IP, collect PTR and passive-DNS results. Passive DNS is high value, and it is exactly where shared hosting misleads.
3. Stage the direct records:
   - A/AAAA -> "resolves to" edges to IP nodes.
   - NS -> nameserver nodes with "uses nameserver" edges.
   - MX/CNAME -> mail and alias nodes; a CNAME target is itself worth pivoting.
   - TXT -> SPF includes and verification tokens.
4. Stage co-resolving domains as candidates with no edge between them.
5. Name what would promote a candidate: a shared certificate, a shared niche nameserver, or a common registrant.

## Rules

- Self-hosted or niche NS -> a real link; mainstream managed DNS -> background.
- Co-resolving domains -> candidates, not links.
- An unusual SPF include or a reused TXT token -> a pivot; a mainstream include -> background.

## Output

- IP nodes, nameserver nodes, mail/alias nodes, and candidate domains.
- For each candidate, the check that would promote it.

## Pitfalls

- Treating shared hosting as an operator link.
- Treating a mainstream nameserver as an actor signal.
- Staging an edge between two domains just because they share an IP.

## Example

```text
a.test has NS ns1.a-hosting.test, and b.test uses the same NS.
If a-hosting.test is a commercial DNS provider with public signup, it is background. No link.
If the nameserver serves only these two domains, it is a signal. Stage the nameserver as a node and add both "uses nameserver" edges to it. There is still no edge between a.test and b.test, because what you observed is a shared server, and the graph should say that.
```

## See also

- "cert-pivot" for certificate siblings.
- "settle" for a candidate that needs a check.

sections.summary: From a certificate/host: shared certificates, CT-log siblings, and shipped defaults.
sections.body:
# Certificate pivot

## Purpose

Use certificate evidence to tie hosts together. Certificates are the strongest pivot in this pack, and the one most often over-interpreted.

## When to use

- You have a certificate, a host, or a CT-log result.
- You need siblings of a host or other hosts that presented the same certificate.
- A self-signed certificate is reused across hosts.

## Procedure

1. Read the leaf certificate's SANs. Each SAN is a sibling worth a node and a "shares certificate" edge.
2. Search CT logs by SHA-256 fingerprint for other hosts that presented it.
3. Search by domain for other certificates the domain has issued.
4. For a self-signed certificate, count the hosts that present it.
5. Decide whether it is operator-generated or shipped with the software.
6. Stage "shares certificate" edges only on a fingerprint match.

## Rules

- Same SHA-256 -> same certificate -> a real link.
- Same issuer -> not a link; Let's Encrypt has issued for a large part of the web.
- A self-signed certificate is either one of the strongest links here or no link at all, depending on who generated it.
- Self-signed, operator-generated (own subject and serial, appears only where they put it, a few hosts) -> strong signal.
- Self-signed, shipped default (product, framework, or device model, on every install nobody reconfigured, many hosts) -> background. The exact fingerprint match is what links unrelated hosts.
- notBefore in the week the infrastructure went up -> made for it; years earlier -> not made for this deployment. It came with the software, or the operator carried it over.
- If nothing can count the hosts, say so and use the subject, issuer, serial, and notBefore checks. Do the subject and issuer name a product, framework, or device model, or nothing at all? Is the serial published as a default? Then it is a default until the count says otherwise.

## Output

- "shares certificate" edges for matching fingerprints.
- A default classification with the count and the evidence. On a default, say which default it is.
- A list of SANs worth pivoting.

## Pitfalls

- An edge on a shared issuer.
- A shipped default treated as an operator certificate.
- A CT-log search treated as a count for a self-signed certificate; CT logs do not record them.

## Example

```text
Two hosts both present a certificate issued by "R11, Let's Encrypt".
WRONG: a "shares certificate" edge. They share an issuer, which is background.
RIGHT: no edge. Compare fingerprints. If they match, the edge is correct and strong.
```

## See also

- "cdn-origin" for certificate reuse at the origin.
- "settle" for a certificate candidate.

sections.summary: From an IP: the announcing AS and its neighbourhood.
sections.body:
# ASN pivot

## Purpose

Place an IP in its announcing AS and bound where else the operator's addresses could be.

## When to use

- You have an IP and need the ASN, the operator's other prefixes, or a size check.
- You need to decide whether a shared AS is meaningful or background.

## Procedure

1. Resolve the IP's ASN (number and name).
2. Stage or reuse an autonomous_system node with an "announced by" edge.
3. List the AS's other announced prefixes.
4. Use those prefixes as a search space, not as links.
5. Check the AS size before treating it as a cluster.

## Size test

- Small operator-run AS, a handful of prefixes -> a meaningful cluster.
- Hyperscaler AS (AS15169, AS16509, AS13335, and peers) -> background.
- A shared AS alone -> never an edge between two IPs.

## Output

- An AS node and an "announced by" edge.
- A bounded search space of prefixes.
- A size judgement with the prefix count.

## Pitfalls

- A shared AS treated as an operator link.
- A hyperscaler treated as a cluster.
- The prefix list treated as a set of links instead of a search space.

## Example

```text
Two of the project's IPs are both announced by AS13335 (Cloudflare).
WRONG: any edge between them, or an "infrastructure cluster" conclusion.
RIGHT: an "announced by" edge from each IP to the AS node, and a sentence saying the shared AS is background here. If both were announced by a two-prefix AS whose name matches the subject organisation, say so. That is a cluster worth reporting.
```

## See also

- "settle" for a candidate in the range.
- "discipline" for the size and population test.

sections.summary: From a URL: build hashes and account identifiers that show what a site serves and who is billed.
sections.body:
# Web footprint

## Purpose

Group hosts by what they serve and by who is billed for the traffic. A phishing kit, a scam portal, or a darknet storefront is usually a build, and the build is the fingerprint.

## When to use

- You have a URL and need to cluster it with the same build.
- You need to find the accounts behind a site.
- You need to decide whether two pages share a kit or only a template.

## Procedure

1. Fingerprint the build: take favicon_hash, hhhash, and dom_hash for the URL (Web Recon pack, desktop only; the probe does the fetching).
2. Search each rare hash with the query plugin's syntax.
3. Compare the three as one observation, not three independent agreements.
4. Read account identifiers from the markup: publisher ID, analytics property, affiliate code, payment account.
5. Count the sites carrying each identifier.
6. Apply the service and money thresholds.
7. Prefer files (/ads.txt, /app-ads.txt, /.well-known/*) over markup tags.

## Hashes

- favicon_hash: MurmurHash3 of the served favicon. Low entropy. Default templates (WordPress defaults, theme demos, boilerplate) are used by thousands of unrelated sites. A rare favicon reused across hosts is a real cluster.
- hhhash: hash of the HTTP header set. The same header set means the same stack and often the same kit. At a CDN, different stacks behind the same front are normal.
- dom_hash: hash of the DOM structure. The strongest of the three. Two pages built from the same kit share a skeleton even after the text and images are swapped.
- A hash is a search key, not just a match. The rare hash that matched two hosts also enumerates the whole population. Read the query plugin's syntax for the field name; vendors take different forms of the hash, and the collecting plugin stores every form it can compute. Do not assume a vendor wants a form you have not collected.
- A title search and a hash search see different host sets. A cluster closed without taking any of its content hashes is not closed.

## Hash rules

- One deployment of one kit sets the favicon, the header set, and the DOM together. Two of three matching is usually one fact observed twice, not two facts agreeing.
- A stock favicon groups nobody, however exactly it matches. A dom_hash from a custom build groups the sites built from it.
- Stage "shares a build" only on a rare match, and name the hash that carried it.
- Never stage "same operator" from a build. A kit is sold, leaked, and copied, and the buyers are strangers to each other.
- Record the capture date. A kit that rotates its favicon every week defeats a single capture.

## Account identifiers

- The Ad Tags pack (desktop only) takes a web.url, an infrastructure.domain, or an infrastructure.ip_address. It reads third-party account identifiers from the markup: an ad-network publisher ID, an analytics property, an affiliate code, a payment account. Those name who is billed for the traffic, which is a different and usually stronger claim than a build match.
- A kit is sold, leaked, and copied, so two buyers are strangers. A monetisation account is where money arrives; reopening one costs identity documents and a payout history. This pivot still works after the domain, the host, and the certificate have changed.
- Values arrive namespaced as `provider:identifier`. Half of these networks issue a bare five-to-nine-digit integer, and an un-namespaced 4823917 would merge one operator's ad zone with an unrelated operator's.
- Every site carrying an identifier is an edge into that node, so the node's edge count is the base rate. Stop guessing and read it.
- A service token (analytics property, tag-manager container, site-verification token) above about 15 sites is a marketing agency's account installed across every client it has, or a site-builder template shipping with its author's container. Do not merge on it. Say AGENCY-SUSPECT and move on. One shared analytics ID can join a gambling network to a forex network and make the graph look like a discovery.
- A money account (advertising, affiliate, payment) can have far more sites before the innocent explanation wins, because holding it is a much stronger reason to be one party. Above about 40 sites it looks like a reseller or a network rather than an operator.
- Files beat tags. /ads.txt, /app-ads.txt, and /.well-known/* sit at fixed paths on the host's own document root and cannot be injected, so an account declared there is the operator's own claim. Prefer them, and say which of the two you have.
- The measured hit rate on hostile hosts is low (about 1 in 10 for /.well-known/assetlinks.json). Absence there means nothing at all, and a bot challenge means less than nothing.

## Output

- "shares a build" edges on a rare match, with the hash that carried it.
- Account nodes with counts and a service or money classification.
- A candidate list for values that do not settle.

## Pitfalls

- A stock favicon or default template treated as a cluster.
- Two of three treated as independent agreement.
- Merging on a shared analytics ID.
- Treating absence in .well-known as evidence.
- Treating a hash as timeless.
- Staging "same operator" from a kit.

## Example

```text
Six streaming mirrors share one analytics property, already linked to 60 sites in the graph.
WRONG: a "same operator" cluster of six. The count says this is somebody's agency account.
RIGHT: no merge. Report the property as AGENCY-SUSPECT with the count, then look for what the six do not share with the other 54. An ad-network zone ID or an affiliate code carried by those six alone is the finding, and it is a money account, not a service token.
Two scam pages share a favicon.
WRONG: a "same operator" edge. The favicon is a free template used by half the internet.
RIGHT: a favicon_hash node with a "serves" edge from each URL, then compare dom_hash and the header set. A rare DOM skeleton on both means "shares a build" edges, naming the hash that carried it. A stock favicon and nothing else means candidates, with what would settle them.
```

## See also

- "cdn-origin" for the origin behind the front.
- "settle" for a candidate value.

sections.summary: From a host behind a CDN/WAF: find the origin, then confirm it serves the site.
sections.body:
# CDN origin

## Purpose

Find the origin behind a CDN/WAF and confirm that it serves the site. Candidates are cheap; confirmation is expensive. The confirm step is the core of this section, not the list.

## When to use

- A host is behind a CDN/WAF and the question is what is behind the front.
- You have a candidate origin and need to confirm it.
- You need the passive routes and the authorization rules for active checks.

## Passive routes

1. History. The most reliable route. A CDN is added later, so old DNS and old snapshots often still show the pre-CDN A record (Wayback CDX, the "historical" hop; VirusTotal resolutions or OTX passive DNS where installed). Dedicated passive-DNS history sites (ipchaxun, ip138, viewdns) and, for Cloudflare, the CrimeFlare dataset hold the same answer. This project has no pack for those collectors, so name the hop you cannot take instead of filling it from memory.
2. DNS leaks. Records domain_recon already pulls, read for an origin the front does not cover: an SPF "ip4:" or "include:" naming an app or mail host; an MX host (mail is rarely proxied, so resolve its A record); a DMARC "rua" or "ruf" host; an AAAA that answers directly because the origin was never v6-fronted.
3. CNAME. The "Detect CDN (Hostname)" target. A target that is not the CDN's own domain (origin.example-hosting.test, a bare "origin" label, a different provider's DNS) is the origin or a hint at it.
4. Certificate. SANs on the leaf often list a management hostname that the public name does not (cert-pivot). The leaf's serial or SHA-256 is an exact-match key: a host presenting the same leaf is the same server, so search for it (Shodan "ssl.cert.serial:" or the fingerprint; VirusTotal). Censys, FOFA, ZoomEye, Quake, and Hunter also index hosts by certificate and favicon, and are collectors this project lacks. Name that hop; on desktop, a WebSearch/WebFetch of their public result pages is the weaker fallback.
5. Subdomains. CT-log enumeration (domain_recon's CT hop) for "origin.", "direct.", "backend.", and "admin." labels. These are names operators give the thing behind the front.
6. Fingerprint search. A rare favicon_hash or DOM/header hash (web-footprint) is also a search key. Another host serving the same rare favicon is an origin candidate, through the same certificate and favicon search packs above. A stock favicon groups nobody (see "discipline").
7. Markup and source leaks. A hardcoded IP in the page's JS or HTML, an exposed "/.env" or "phpinfo", a GA/AdSense ID (Ad Tags), or the domain named in public code (GitHub pack, or the agent's own web search). Weak alone: a candidate, never proof.

## Confirm the origin

This check replaces any grade or percentage.
1. Send a request directly to the candidate with the target's Host header.
2. Match dom_hash, title, or body, not just a 200; any host answers 200.
3. Require one independent binding: the same leaf certificate serial on the candidate, its PTR or passive-DNS naming the target, or a non-CDN Server header on a port a CDN edge never opens (22/21).
4. Stage the origin as its own node with evidence-labelled edges ("was hosted at", "presents certificate", "serves the site"), never "operated by". The analyst decides who runs it.
A candidate that only sits in the right ASN or the right country is not confirmed; most hosts share that.

## Active routes

Run these only on the desktop build, with the analyst's command and probe tools enabled, at the analyst's explicit instruction, and only against a target the analyst is authorized to test. If any of those is missing, name the hop you did not take instead of describing it as done.
- The direct Host-header fetch the confirm step already needs.
- A candidate port sweep for the CDN-passthrough ports (2052/2053/2082/2083/8443/8080...) and for the SSH/FTP a CDN edge never opens.
- A /24 sweep around a confirmed candidate.
- Request shaping against the front (Host override, X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP, method or path variance, an oversized body) to elicit an origin response.
- An AXFR zone transfer or DNSSEC NSEC walk against the authoritative nameserver.
- EDNS client-subnet (dig +subnet) and multi-resolver queries for a nearer answer.
- Traceroute/MTR for the last hop before the CDN.
None of these upgrades a guess. A hop that runs must still follow the confirm rules above, and stages only evidence-labelled candidates.

## Output

- An origin node with "was hosted at", "presents certificate", and "serves the site" edges.
- Never "operated by"; the analyst draws that.
- A list of active hops not taken, with the reason.

## Pitfalls

- Treating the front as the host.
- Treating a 200 as proof.
- Treating the right ASN or country as confirmation.
- Running active checks without desktop, authorization, or instruction.

## Example

```text
cdncheck says example.test is behind Cloudflare.
WRONG: "behind a CDN, so there is nothing more to see." The front is not the host.
RIGHT: Wayback shows 203.0.113.9 as example.test's A record before the CDN was added. Fetched with curl --resolve example.test:443:203.0.113.9, that IP serves the same DOM and presents a leaf whose serial matches the public certificate and whose SAN lists origin.example.test. Serves the site plus a certificate binding: stage the IP with "was hosted at", "presents certificate", and "serves the site" edges. Only the analyst decides what that says about who runs it.
```

## See also

- "settle" for a candidate origin.
- "historical" for pre-CDN records.

sections.summary: From a domain/URL: what old snapshots show that the current page does not.
sections.body:
# Historical

## Purpose

Use old snapshots to recover what the current page hides.

## When to use

- The current page is clean but the history matters.
- The CDN is new and you need the pre-CDN record.
- The kit, contacts, or C2 changed over time.
- A defacement or takeover is part of the question.

## Procedure

1. Use the Wayback Machine pack ("Wayback Snapshot History", "Wayback Availability"). Pull the earliest snapshot, the latest, and snapshots around the date of interest.
2. Read for pre-CDN A records, defacement or takeover history, kit evolution, and old contacts. Footers and registration pages in old snapshots often carry an email or handle the current page dropped.
3. Label every edge with the date.
4. Do not upgrade a "was" edge without a current observation.
5. Hand off to "Account & identity pivoting" when a snapshot names a person, an email, or a handle.

## Labelling rules

- "was" edge -> a statement about the snapshot date, not today.
- Defacement -> evidence of the past, not of the current operator.
- Old contact -> a handoff, not an attribution.

## Output

- Dated edges, with the snapshot date and the evidence.
- Old contacts for the identity pack.
- A clear statement of what is not claimed about the current operator.

## Pitfalls

- Treating a snapshot as current.
- Attributing the current operator from a defacement.
- Upgrading a "was" edge without a current observation.

## Example

```text
The defaced site now shows a clean page.
WRONG: "the group operated example.test." The snapshot shows the defacement, not the operator.
RIGHT: record the snapshot's content on the url node, stage the group name only where a second source corroborates it, and add a dated "was defaced by" edge. Do not claim who the current operator is.
```

## See also

- "cdn-origin" for the pre-CDN origin.
- "Account & identity pivoting" for a person, email, or handle.

starters.label: Expand one indicator
starters.summary: From one IP, domain, or certificate to the infrastructure around it.
starters.prompt:
Expand the infrastructure around {{indicator}}. What else is connected to it?
Context: {{context}}.
Work one verified hop at a time and stage a node or edge for each. Label each one for the evidence, not the conclusion. Read "discipline" first and stop where you should. Then read the section for the hop you are on.

variables.label: What you already know (optional)
variables.placeholder: seen in a phishing kit, first observed last week

starters.label: Map a domain
starters.summary: DNS and certificate hops from one domain, with branches that stop early called out.
starters.prompt:
Starting from the domain {{domain}}, work the DNS records and certificate siblings and map what you can corroborate.
If a hop needs a collection plugin this project does not have, say which hop you cannot take instead of filling it from memory.
Read "dns-pivot" and "cert-pivot".

starters.label: Start from a certificate
starters.summary: SANs and CT-log siblings: the strongest pivot in the pack, and the easiest to over-interpret.
starters.prompt:
Start from the certificate {{cert}}.
List its SANs and, from the transparency logs, the other hosts that presented it. Stage a sibling for each corroborated host with a "shares certificate" edge. Tell me which of these look like one operator and which look like a shared CA default.
Read "cert-pivot".

starters.label: Explore an AS neighbourhood
starters.summary: Find where else an operator's addresses could be, without treating a shared AS as a link.
starters.prompt:
Take {{asn}} and describe the neighbourhood it defines: who announces it, how large it is, and whether it is an operator network or background infrastructure.
Then check it against the other indicators in this project. Stage an edge only where a concrete indicator connects them. A shared AS on its own is not a connection.
Read "asn-pivot".

variables.label: ASN or an IP inside it

starters.label: Triage a list of indicators
starters.summary: One hop on each indicator, to find the few that deserve a deeper look.
starters.prompt:
Here is a list of indicators: {{indicators}}.
Take one hop on each and tell me which are worth pursuing and which are background infrastructure. Do not go deep on any of them yet. The point is to find where a deeper look is worth it.
Read "discipline" and "background-values". The background-versus-signal check is the whole task here.

starters.label: Related, or just shared hosting?
starters.summary: The question this pack exists to answer carefully.
starters.prompt:
Two indicators: {{a}} and {{b}}.
Tell me whether the evidence ties them to one operator, or whether what they share is used by thousands of unrelated parties. Give me the estimate, not just the verdict: how many others have each shared attribute and what that rests on, which attributes could have come from a single act rather than independent agreement, and what would settle it.
Read "discipline" first, then "background-values" for the shared value, then "settle" for the check.

starters.label: Check a link the project already draws
starters.summary: Audit an existing edge against the evidence behind it.
starters.prompt:
This project links {{a}} to {{b}} with the label "{{label}}".
Check whether the evidence supports that label, a weaker one, or nothing at all. If the label claims more than the evidence does, say what label it should have instead. Say how many unrelated parties would share what this rests on, and run the check that would settle it instead of describing it.
Read "discipline", then "background-values" for the shared value, then "settle".

starters.label: Strip out shared-hosting noise
starters.summary: Find links in this project that rest only on background infrastructure.
starters.prompt:
Go over the infrastructure already in this project and find the links that rest only on an attribute used by thousands: shared hosting, a CDN front, a mainstream registrar, a hyperscaler AS, a common CA.
For each, say how many unrelated parties have it and what that rests on. Then tell me which links should be removed, which should be relabelled to what they actually observed, and which are fine. Do not remove anything without saying why.
Read "discipline" and "background-values".

starters.label: Summarise the footprint
starters.summary: The chain so far, with each hop's evidence and each branch that stopped.
starters.prompt:
Summarise the infrastructure footprint this project has established around {{subject}}.
Walk the chain hop by hop with the evidence behind each, and name the branches that stopped. Say whether each stopped because it ran out of signal or because no installed plugin could take the hop. Those are different, and only one of them is finished.
Report in the form the overview describes.

starters.label: What is left to check?
starters.summary: Turn unfinished branches into a ranked list of next hops.
starters.prompt:
List the hops this project has not taken yet, ranked by how much the footprint would narrow if you took them.
Run the ones this project's installed plugins can answer instead of listing them. Say plainly which ones nothing here can reach.
Read "settle" and "prioritize".

starters.label: Fingerprint a URL
starters.summary: Group a page with the builds it shares: favicon, header, and DOM hashes.
starters.prompt:
Fingerprint the URL {{url}} with its favicon, header set, and DOM structure. Tell me what else in this project shares a build with it.
If a fingerprint hop needs a plugin this project does not have (Web Recon is desktop-only), say which hop you cannot take.
Read "web-footprint".

starters.label: Find the origin behind a CDN
starters.summary: What is really serving the site behind the Cloudflare/Akamai front.
starters.prompt:
The host {{host}} is behind a CDN or WAF. Find what is really behind the front using CNAME hints, historical records, certificate SANs, and CT-log subdomains. Stage the origin as a candidate, not a conclusion.
Read "cdn-origin".

starters.label: What did it look like before?
starters.summary: Wayback hops: defacement, pre-CDN state, old contacts, and kit evolution.
starters.prompt:
Pull the history of {{url}}: the earliest snapshot, the most recent one, and any snapshot around {{around}}.
Tell me what the past shows that today hides, with every finding dated. If a snapshot names a person, an email, or a handle, hand off to Account & identity pivoting instead of attributing here.
Read "historical".
